import nbformat
p='notebooks/Edwards-A10.ipynb'
nb=nbformat.read(p,4)
M=nbformat.v4.new_markdown_cell; C=nbformat.v4.new_code_cell
cells=[
M('''## 7. The remaining inputs

Same review as §6 for the other input columns: `fin_budget`, release timing, `mpaa_rating`, `director`, `writer`, `original_language`, `franchise`, `source_material`. Values and spread only; no outcome yet.'''),
M('### 7a. `fin_budget`\n\nThe production budget (the contract allows it as an input). Shown: spread, budget tiers, round-number budgets, and the smallest and largest.'),
C('''b = cu["fin_budget"]
display(numeric_profile(cu, ["fin_budget"]))
profile_grid([(np.log10(b), "log10 fin_budget", "log10 $ (6 = $1M, 8 = $100M)", False)], "films", ncols=1)
btier = pd.cut(b, [0, 5e6, 20e6, 60e6, 150e6, np.inf], labels=["$1-5M", "$5-20M", "$20-60M", "$60-150M", "$150M+"])
display(btier.value_counts().sort_index().rename("films").to_frame().assign(**{"% of films": lambda d: (100 * d["films"] / n_u).round(1)}))
print(f"Budgets that are a round $1M: {(b % 1e6 == 0).mean():.0%}")
print("Source:"); display(cu["fin_budget_src"].value_counts().rename("films").to_frame())
show = ["title", "year", "fin_budget", "fin_budget_src", "runtime_min"]
print("Largest:"); display(cu.nlargest(8, "fin_budget")[show])'''),
M('### 7b. Release timing: `release_date`, `release_month`, `release_quarter`\n\nUS release date, falling back to TMDB\'s first release. Shown: films by month and year, and how often the fallback is used.'),
C('''display(cu["release_date_src"].value_counts().rename("films").to_frame())
rm = cu["release_month"].value_counts().sort_index()
display(pd.DataFrame({"films": rm, "% of films": (100 * rm / n_u).round(1)}).T)
yr = cu["year"].value_counts().sort_index()
display(yr.rename("films").to_frame().T)
rd = pd.to_datetime(cu["release_date"], format="mixed", errors="coerce")
print(f"Release year differs from film year: {(rd.dt.year != cu['year']).mean():.1%} of films")
print("Day of week:"); display(rd.dt.day_name().value_counts().rename("films").to_frame().T)'''),
M('### 7c. `mpaa_rating`\n\nThe Numbers → RT → RT sl, standardized. "NR" (not rated) is a real value; blank means no source had one.'),
C('''mr = cu["mpaa_rating"].value_counts(dropna=False)
display(pd.DataFrame({"films": mr, "% of films": (100 * mr / n_u).round(1)}))
print("Blank by budget tier:")
display(cu["mpaa_rating"].isna().groupby(btier, observed=True).mean().map("{:.0%}".format).rename("% blank").to_frame())
print("Blank by original language (top 6):")
top_lang = cu["original_language"].value_counts().head(6).index
display(cu[cu["original_language"].isin(top_lang)].groupby("original_language")["mpaa_rating"].apply(lambda s: f"{s.isna().mean():.0%}").rename("% blank").to_frame())'''),
M('### 7d. `director` and `writer`\n\nPeople only work as an input as a **track record** (how their earlier films did), so the key question is how many films each person has.'),
C('''for col in ["director", "writer"]:
    v = items(col).value_counts()
    print(f"--- {col}: {len(v):,} distinct people across {cu[col].notna().sum():,} films ---")
    print("People per film:"); display(per_film(col).value_counts().sort_index().head(8).rename("films").to_frame().T)
    print("How many films each person appears in:"); display(films_per_value(col))
    print("Top 10:"); display(v.head(10).rename("films").to_frame().T)
both = cu[["director", "writer"]].dropna()
same = both.apply(lambda r: bool(set(t.strip() for t in r["director"].split(",")) & set(t.strip() for t in r["writer"].split(","))), axis=1)
print(f"Director also credited as writer: {same.mean():.0%} of films with both")'''),
M('### 7e. `original_language`\n\nTMDB → RT, ISO codes.'),
C('''ol = cu["original_language"].value_counts(dropna=False)
display(pd.DataFrame({"films": ol, "% of films": (100 * ol / n_u).round(1)}).head(15))
print(f"{cu['original_language'].nunique()} distinct languages")
print("English vs countries (does the US flag already cover it?):")
us = cu["countries"].fillna("").str.contains("United States")
display(pd.crosstab(cu["original_language"].eq("en").map({True: "English", False: "Not English"}), us.map({True: "includes US", False: "no US"}), margins=True))'''),
M('### 7f. `franchise`\n\nThe Numbers only, split into one value per franchise (`|`-separated). Blank means either "not in a franchise" or "not in The Numbers", and the two can\'t be told apart.'),
C('''fr = cu["franchise"].dropna().str.split("|").explode().str.strip()
frc = fr.value_counts()
print(f"{cu['franchise'].notna().mean():.1%} of films have a franchise; {len(frc):,} distinct franchises")
print("Films per franchise:")
display(pd.cut(frc, [0, 1, 2, 4, np.inf], labels=["1", "2", "3-4", "5+"]).value_counts().sort_index().rename("franchises").to_frame().T)
display(frc.head(15).rename("films").to_frame().T)
print("Filled by budget tier:")
display(cu["franchise"].notna().groupby(btier, observed=True).mean().map("{:.0%}".format).rename("% with franchise").to_frame().T)
print("Franchise vs source_material:")
display(pd.crosstab(cu["source_material"].fillna("(blank)"), cu["franchise"].notna().map({True: "franchise", False: "no franchise"})))'''),
M('### 7g. `source_material`\n\nThe Numbers only.'),
C('''sm = cu["source_material"].value_counts(dropna=False)
display(pd.DataFrame({"films": sm, "% of films": (100 * sm / n_u).round(1)}))
print("Blank by budget tier:")
display(cu["source_material"].isna().groupby(btier, observed=True).mean().map("{:.0%}".format).rename("% blank").to_frame().T)
print(f"source_material and creative_type both blank: {(cu['source_material'].isna() & cu['creative_type'].isna()).mean():.0%}; "
      f"only one blank: {(cu['source_material'].isna() ^ cu['creative_type'].isna()).mean():.0%}")'''),
]
nb.cells.extend(cells)
nbformat.write(nb,p)
EOF

# A10 Purpose Contract: proposed amendments (DRAFT)

Proposed by Tanner Edwards, 2026-11-23. **Not in effect.** These are changes to `A10_purpose_contract_FROZEN_2026-11-17.md`, which was frozen by Matt alone. Each one takes effect only when Tanner and Matt both agree. Agreed items are then copied into the contract's **Amendments** section with the date and reason.

| # | Contract field | Current | Proposed | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Population: years | 2000–2023, no reason stated | **Keep 2000–2023**, and record the reason | Proposed |
| A2 | Population: budget floor | Budget ≥ $1M, no sensitivity check | **Keep $1M for the main analysis; rerun at $100K as a sensitivity check.** Budgets under $1K are data errors and are handled in cleaning. | Proposed |
| A3 | Outcome: 2.5× multiple | "Commonly cited rule of thumb" | **Keep 2.5×**, labeled as an industry convention, not a data finding | Proposed |
| A4 | Allowed inputs | Fixed list of 8 | **Re-open after cleaning.** Add every input known at the financing decision. | Open: list to follow |
| A5 | 2020–2023 stress test | COVID years reported separately | Not discussed yet | Open |

## A1. Keep 2000–2023, with a reason
**Reason:** 24 years of films is enough to be relevant to today's market. Before 2000, the data gets thin, and dollar amounts would need inflation adjustment to compare fairly. The end year stays at 2023 because later films hadn't finished their theatrical run when the data was pulled.

## A2. Keep the $1M floor; add a $100K sensitivity check
**Reason to look below $1M:** Low-budget films are part of the financing decision, and they're where the biggest margins happen. Among usable films with a $100K–$1M budget, 14% returned 10× their budget or more, against 4% of films above $1M.

**Reason not to make it the main population:** the S4 rerun (2026-11-23). Revenue is missing far more often below $1M, and the films that are missing it are mostly losers. So the $100K–$1M films we can see lean toward the winners, which probably inflates the 14% figure too.

| Films with a budget | $1M floor | $100K floor | $100K–1M only |
|---|---|---|---|
| Films | 11,212 | 16,065 | 4,853 |
| Missing revenue | 39% | 52% | 83% |
| Missing revenue, 2020–23 | 52% | 69% | 92% |
| Missing-revenue films with US gross < budget* | 98% | 97% | 93% |

\*Among the 3–5% of missing-revenue films that have a US box office figure.

**Proposal:** the main analysis keeps the $1M floor. The final model is rerun on the $100K population (7,671 usable films: train 5,554 / test 1,426 / stress 691; 66.9% losers), and the report shows both results side by side. Any $100K result is limited to "films with reported revenue."

**Also changes:** the plan adds a step for the $100K sensitivity rerun. `00_build_dataset.ipynb` gets a flag for the $100K population (e.g. `usable_100k`) alongside `usable`.

## A3. Label 2.5× as an industry convention
**Reason:** 2.5× is a rule of thumb, not something the data shows. Theaters keep roughly half the box office, and marketing often costs about as much as production, so a film needs about 2–2.5× its budget to break even. The report must say that the threshold is an industry convention, cite a source for it, and show the 1×, 2× and 3× sensitivity results next to it.

## A4. Inputs: re-open the allowed list (pending)
The frozen list allows 8 inputs. The rule behind it stays: **only information known at the financing decision, before production.** The list itself is re-opened. After cleaning, every column that meets the rule is proposed here with its evidence. Candidates so far: MPAA rating, source material, creative type, production method, writer, cast, distributor, franchise / sequel (see `FEATURE_IDEAS.md`).

## A5. COVID-era stress test (not discussed yet)

import nbformat
p='notebooks/Edwards-A10.ipynb'
nb=nbformat.read(p,4)
md='''### 8d. What the outlier checks show (run 2026-11-24), for Tanner's review

**The biggest finding: 929 usable films (14%) exist only in TMDB.** None of The Numbers, Rotten Tomatoes or Box Office Mojo has them, so their budget and revenue (and so the label) come only from TMDB's user-edited data. Almost every other rule mostly catches these same films. They are a mix:
- Junk: *Skibidi Toilet: The Movie*, *Adventures in Bora Bora* ($800M, 5 min), *😤 insect james 😤*, fan edits, concert videos.
- Real films, mostly non-English (80%): *Deep Sea* (China), *Death Note: The Last Name* (Japan), *Solomon Kane*.

| Rule | Films | Proposed |
|---|---|---|
| Runtime 400+ min | 12 | **Exclude.** All TV series or video games (*God of War*, *The Bear*, *What If...?*). |
| Runtime under 60 min | 46 | **Exclude.** Anime episodes, clips, junk. A few real IMAX documentaries (*Sea Rex*), which aren't feature films either. |
| TV Movie genre | 14 | **Exclude.** Not theatrical (*High School Musical*, *Stargate: Continuum*); their revenue figures are made up ($5,940). |
| Title says edition / cut / concert / play | 26 | **Exclude**, except theatrical concert films (*Hannah Montana … Concert*, *Glee: The Concert Movie*). Re-release editions duplicate the real film. |
| Music as the only genre | 15 | **Exclude** if TMDB-only (concert videos). |
| No outside source | 929 | **Decision needed** (below). |
| Budget per minute extreme | 25 | **Exclude.** Junk entries; also shows wrong runtimes on real titles. |
| Non-US $100M+ budget | 12 | **Check by hand.** Some are real US dollars (*The Battle at Lake Changjin*, *Detective Chinatown 3*); *Lost in the Stars* and *Chasing the Dragon* look like local currency. |
| Revenue = budget | 18 | **Exclude.** Copied value, not a real revenue. |
| Revenue under $10K | 101 | Keep if an outside source has the film (real tiny releases, e.g. *The Fanatic*); exclude if TMDB-only. |

**Tanner's Music question:** the Music genre is mostly real films about music (*A Star Is Born*, *Crazy Heart*, *Step Up*, *Footloose*). Concert films that played in theaters (*This Is It*, *Justin Bieber: Believe*) are real releases with real box office. Only the TMDB-only concert videos are junk. **Keep the genre; drop the videos.**

**Budget vs runtime:** works for junk at the edges (5-minute films with $100M budgets) but not in the middle. Budget per minute is roughly flat from 80 to 180 minutes.

**Budget by country:** doesn't show currency errors as a group. China has the highest median ($25M). Currency mistakes are individual films, so they need a hand check, not a country rule.

**New matching problem found:** junk TMDB entries that share a real film's title can take the real film's matches. *WONKA* (2023, "Documentary", 11 min) has 3 outside sources and a $125M budget, and *Wish* (2023, Drama, 66 min) has Disney's $200M budget. The real films may be missing or duplicated. Needs a fix in `00_build_dataset.ipynb`.

**Decision for Tanner: the 929 TMDB-only films**
1. **Exclude all** (recommended). The label can't be checked against anything. Cost: loses some real foreign films and makes the data more US-heavy.
2. **Exclude only those caught by another rule** (about 120). Keeps real foreign films, but leaves unverified revenue in the label.
3. **Keep all**, and add `n_sources` as a data-quality flag for a sensitivity check.

**After this:** §9 goes through missing values one column at a time.
'''
nb.cells.append(nbformat.v4.new_markdown_cell(md))
nbformat.write(nb,p)
EOF

**The main finding: 929 usable films (14%) exist only in TMDB.** None of The Numbers, Rotten Tomatoes or Box Office Mojo has them, so their budget and revenue, and therefore their loser label, can't be checked. Most of the other rules end up catching these same films.
- Some are junk, like *Skibidi Toilet: The Movie*, or *Adventures in Bora Bora* at $800M for 5 minutes.
- Some are real films, mostly non-English (80%).

Apart from that group, the other rules catch 223 films (3.3%). I propose excluding:
- TV series and games
- entries under 60 minutes
- TV movies
- re-release editions and fan cuts
- revenue copied from budget

**Your Music question:** the genre is mostly real films about music, like *A Star Is Born* and *Step Up*. Concert films that played in theaters are real releases. Only the concert videos that exist only in TMDB are junk. So keep the genre and drop those videos.

**Your two budget ideas:** they partly worked.
- **Budget vs runtime:** catches junk at the edges, such as 5-minute "films" with $100M budgets, but not in the middle.
- **Budget by country:** doesn't reveal currency errors as a group. They're individual films, like *Lost in the Stars* and *Chasing the Dragon*, so they need a check by hand.

**A new bug in the build:** the real *Wonka* and *Wish* were still marked "Post Production" in the TMDB snapshot, so the build skipped them. Nothing is committed yet.

**Decision for you: what do we do with the 929 TMDB-only films?**
1. **Exclude them all (my recommendation).** Their label can't be verified. The cost is losing some real foreign films.

# budget/revenue
u['br']=u.fin_budget/u.fin_revenue

content.text:
I recorded "drop everything under 60 minutes." I tested your currency idea first, and it led somewhere slightly different.

**Currency**

The problem with converting is that we don't know which currency a budget was entered in, so there's nothing to convert from. What we can check is where two sources disagree. 3,921 usable films have a budget from both TMDB and The Numbers (or Wikidata):
- 80% agree within 10%.
- Big gaps show up in US films as much as foreign ones. Examples: *Awake* is $86M vs $8.6M, an extra zero; *The Chaser* is $120M vs $2.6M.

So the bigger problem is typos in TMDB's budgets, not currency. The build also uses TMDB's budget first when sources disagree.

**My proposal:**
1. When the two budgets differ by more than 2×, use The Numbers instead of TMDB. That fixes about 70 films with no hand checking.
2. For foreign films with only one budget source, make your scatter plot: budget vs revenue, US vs non-US. Hand-check only the few that sit far out from the rest.

**Revenue under $10K (75 films)**

Your rating idea splits them cleanly:

| Rating | Films |
|---|---|
| Real MPAA rating (R, PG-13, PG, G) | 50 |
| NR | 15 |
| Blank | 10 |

Proposal: keep the 50 rated films as real low grossers, and drop the 25 NR or blank ones.

Do you agree with both proposals?

"""Download the A10 raw datasets from Kaggle into data/raw/.

Run from the repo root:  python tools/get_data.py
Files are gitignored; every collaborator runs this once on their own machine.
data/raw/ is treated as read-only after download — never edit these files.
"""
import shutil
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

import truststore

# Use the OS certificate store so downloads work behind TLS-inspecting proxies (e.g. Zscaler)
truststore.inject_into_ssl()

import kagglehub  # noqa: E402

RAW = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data" / "raw"

# Kaggle handle -> (subfolder of data/raw, files expected). Recorded in the Data Receipt.
# stefanoleone992 gets its own subfolder: its rotten_tomatoes_movies.csv shares a
# filename with the (different) andrezaza file Matt's plan already uses.
DATASETS = {
    "asaniczka/tmdb-movies-dataset-2023-930k-movies": ("", ["TMDB_movie_dataset_v11.csv"]),
    "priyamchoksi/rotten-tomato-movie-reviews-1-44m-rows": ("", ["rotten_tomatoes_movie_reviews.csv"]),
    "andrezaza/clapper-massive-rotten-tomatoes-movies-and-reviews": ("", ["rotten_tomatoes_movies.csv"]),
    "stefanoleone992/rotten-tomatoes-movies-and-critic-reviews-dataset": (
        "stefanoleone992",
        ["rotten_tomatoes_movies.csv", "rotten_tomatoes_critic_reviews.csv"],
    ),
    # Scraped from the-numbers.com: budget, domestic/intl/worldwide gross, plus pre-release fields
    "michaelmatta0/movies-ultimate-metrics-features-and-metadata": (
        "the_numbers",
        ["Top Movies (Cleaned Data).csv"],
    ),
}

# Non-Kaggle direct downloads: (subfolder, filename) -> URL
URL_FILES = {
    # Box Office Mojo daily domestic grosses, scraped by github.com/tjwaterman99/boxofficemojo-scraper
    ("boxofficemojo", "revenues_per_day.csv.gz"):
        "https://github.com/tjwaterman99/boxofficemojo-scraper/releases/latest/download/revenues_per_day.csv.gz",
}


def main() -> None:
    RAW.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for (subdir, name), url in URL_FILES.items():
        print(f"\n== {url}")
        dst = RAW / subdir / name
        dst.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        if dst.exists():
            print(f"  exists, skipping: {name}")
            continue
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, dst)
        print(f"  downloaded {name} ({dst.stat().st_size / 1e6:,.0f} MB)")
    for handle, (subdir, wanted) in DATASETS.items():
        print(f"\n== {handle}")
        src = Path(kagglehub.dataset_download(handle))
        dest_dir = RAW / subdir
        dest_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        for name in wanted:
            dst = dest_dir / name
            if dst.exists():
                print(f"  exists, skipping: {dst.name}")
                continue
            matches = list(src.rglob(name))
            if not matches:
                available = sorted(p.name for p in src.rglob("*") if p.is_file())
                print(f"  NOT FOUND: {name}. Files in download: {available}")
                continue
            shutil.copy2(matches[0], dst)
            print(f"  copied {name} ({dst.stat().st_size / 1e6:,.0f} MB)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

    "priyamchoksi/rotten-tomato-movie-reviews-1-44m-rows": ("", ["rotten_tomatoes_movie_reviews.csv"]),
    "andrezaza/clapper-massive-rotten-tomatoes-movies-and-reviews": ("", ["rotten_tomatoes_movies.csv"]),
    "stefanoleone992/rotten-tomatoes-movies-and-critic-reviews-dataset": (
        "stefanoleone992",
        ["rotten_tomatoes_movies.csv", "rotten_tomatoes_critic_reviews.csv"],

    # Scraped from the-numbers.com: budget, domestic/intl/worldwide gross, plus pre-release fields
    "michaelmatta0/movies-ultimate-metrics-features-and-metadata": (

    ),
}

    ("boxofficemojo", "revenues_per_day.csv.gz"):

}


def main() -> None:
    RAW.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for (subdir, name), url in URL_FILES.items():
        print(f"\n== {url}")
        dst = RAW / subdir / name
        dst.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        if dst.exists():
            print(f"  exists, skipping: {name}")
            continue
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, dst)
        print(f"  downloaded {name} ({dst.stat().st_size / 1e6:,.0f} MB)")
    for handle, (subdir, wanted) in DATASETS.items():

                print(f"  NOT FOUND: {name}. Files in download: {available}")

content.text:
The test worked for directors and writers but not for distributors. It also turned up a matching bug. I queried 200 films: 100 with blanks to test filling, and 100 complete ones to test accuracy.

| Column | Blanks filled | Agrees with our data | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| director | 12 of 12 | 96% | **Use it** |
| writer | 15 of 18 | 97% | **Use it** |
| runtime | (no blanks in sample) | 96% within 5 min | Use it for the 28 blanks |
| distributor | 12 of 18 | — | **Don't use.** It lists every distributor worldwide plus streamers (Netflix, Hulu, Italy's Eagle Pictures), not the US theatrical one. |
| source_material | 18 of 84 | — | Partial. It only says "based on X"; no entry could mean original or unknown. |
| production_companies | 0 of 3 | — | No help |
| creative_type | — | — | Doesn't exist there |

**The matching bug:** where Wikidata disagreed with us, our row was mixing two different films with the same title:
- *Barbecue* (2014): our director is from an Australian documentary, but the film is a French comedy.
- *Simon* (2004): the same kind of mix.

So the Wikidata comparison doubles as a check for bad matches in the build.

**My recommendation:**
1. Pull director, writer and runtime from Wikidata for all films. That fills about 470 blanks.
2. Flag every film where Wikidata's director disagrees with ours as a possible mismatch, for review.
3. For source material, fill only "based on a book / comic / etc." where Wikidata has it.
4. Leave distributor and creative type blank, with "was missing" flags.

Should I go ahead with the full pull?

"""
import datetime as dt
import json
import time
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
import truststore

truststore.inject_into_ssl()

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
QUERY = (ROOT / "tools" / "wikidata_people.rq").read_text()

BATCH = 200


def run(ids: list[str]) -> list[dict]:
    q = QUERY.replace("{IDS}", " ".join(f'"{i}"' for i in ids))
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        "https://query.wikidata.org/sparql",

content.text:
Yes, mostly. TMDB keywords cover 90% of the blanks, and there's good news for your comic-book hypothesis.

**Test:** I grouped the source material into your categories and compared the keywords with The Numbers on 3,801 films where both exist. Overall they agree 74% of the time.

| Keywords say | The Numbers agrees | Blanks this would fill |
|---|---|---|
| Book | 89% | 59 |
| Other adaptation (TV, game, play, toy…) | 89% | 14 |
| Real life | 78% | 85 |
| Comic | 72% (and they find 93% of the real comic films) | 15 |
| Original | 72% | 596 |
| Remake | 50% | 30 |
| No keywords | — | 92 |

**For your hypothesis:** only 15 of the blanks look like comic-book films. The Numbers already covers comic films well, since they're big releases. The blanks are mostly small films.

**The weak spot is "Original."** For films with no source keyword, about 1 in 4 are actually adaptations that nobody tagged. That's 596 of the blanks.

**My proposal:**
1. Add a grouped column, `source_group`, for every film: Comic, Book, Real life, Remake, Other adaptation, Original. This also replaces The Numbers' 23 small categories.
2. Fill the blanks from the keywords.
3. Mark each filled value with where it came from, so we can rerun the model with and without the keyword guesses.

One decision: should the 596 keyword "Originals" be filled as Original, or left as unknown?

    if has("based on comic", "superhero", "based on graphic novel", "based on manga", "comic book", "based on webcomic", "based on cartoon"):
        return "Comic"
    if has("remake", "reboot", "based on movie", "based on short film"):

    if has("based on true story", "biography", "biographical", "based on memoir", "autobiograph"):

# A10 Project Purpose Contract — FROZEN 2026-11-17

Date drafted: 2026-11-17. Analyst: Matt Sorensen. AI role: Problem Setter, then Challenger (Claude Code, decision-statement-builder skill).
Source candidate: #1 in `report/A10_problem_scan_2026-11-17.md`.
Status: **FROZEN 2026-11-17, approved by Matt Sorensen.** This was done before any analysis of how inputs relate to the outcome; only structural profiling and join tests have been run. Any later change requires a dated amendment, added below, with a stated reason.

## Contract fields

| Field | Contract answer |
|---|---|
| **Purpose pathway** | **Predictive** (the one primary path). An explanatory layer reports how much director track record adds to the prediction. That's association only, with no causal claim. |
| **Decision** | At the financing stage, before production, the acquisitions team decides for each incoming project whether to **flag for deep review**, **proceed on standard review**, or **pass**. |
| **Action** | Each year, the 20% of projects with the highest predicted risk go to deep review (comparable-film analysis, a second reader, renegotiating terms). The rest get standard review. The screen never rejects a project on its own. |
| **Decision time** | When the financing decision is made, before production. **Allowed inputs:** budget, genre, director's track record from earlier films only, production companies' track record from earlier films only, planned runtime, planned release month and quarter, original language, product
| **Population & unit** | Unit = **one feature film at its financing decision.** Population = feature films released 2000–2023 with a reported budget ≥ $1M and reported worldwide revenue > 0, excluding adult titles. Training: 2000–2015. Test: 2016–2019. Stress test: 2020–2023 (COVID era), reported s
| **Outcome / target & horizon** | Positive class = **"money-loser": worldwide revenue < 2.5 × budget.** The 2.5× multiple is a labeled assumption (a commonly cited rule of thumb for covering marketing and the exhibitor's share). It's rerun at 1×, 2× and 3× as a sensitivity check. Horizon = full the
| **Baseline** | (a) **Random 20% flagging**, which catches losers at the base rate (the floor). (b) **A simple rule:** flag projects in the genre × budget-tier groups with the highest historical loss rate, using training years only. The model has to beat (b), not just (a). |
| **Evidence standard** | On the 2016–2019 test films, the share of all money-losers that fall inside the flagged top 20% (capture rate). The model must beat rule (b) by **≥ 5 percentage points**, with a bootstrap 95% CI that excludes 0. Also report precision at 20%, calibration, and the result for 
| **Value** | More money-losers reach deep review without adding review workload: same 20% capacity, better targeting. content.content:
--- 0
# 00 · Build the unified dataset

**Shared pipeline notebook (team-owned).** Run it once after `tools/get_data.py`, and again whenever this notebook or the raw data changes. Changes go through a PR.

**Outputs** (both gitignored, so each person builds their own copy):
- `data/clean/films_unified.csv`: **one row per film** with every source attached, keyed by `film_uid`. Includes per-film review summaries (`rtrev_*`, `slrev_*`).
- `data/clean/reviews_unified.csv`: **one row per critic review** (one film has many), keyed by `film_uid` (§9b).

**`film_uid`** is the stable key: `tmdb-<TMDB id>`, or `tn-<The Numbers URL slug>` for films not in TMDB. It doesn't change between rebuilds. All other notebooks start from this file instead of re-merging.

| Source | Adds | Join |
|---|---|---|
| TMDB | Base table: one row per TMDB id | — |
| The Numbers | Budget, **worldwide** gross, MPAA, source, franchise, companies | Title + year matcher (§4, hand-checked 50/50) plus a looser second pass (§4b) |
| Wikidata snapshot (committed) | Budget and box office in USD | TMDB id |
| Box Office Mojo | Domestic gross, theaters (US theatrical run) | Title + year matcher |
| RT stefanoleone992 | `actors`, `production_company` | Title + year matcher |
| RT andrezaza | Director, writer, RT box office, ratings | Matt's join rules (§7), hand-checked 0/50 wrong |

**Combined financials:** `fin_budget` / `fin_revenue` take the first available value from TMDB → The Numbers → Wikidata; `fin_*_src` records which. `usable` = 2000–2023, budget ≥ $1M, revenue > 0.

Rows not in TMDB (The Numbers only) have a **negative `id`** (not stable across rebuilds; use `film_uid`) and `in_tmdb` = False.

Column prefixes: none = TMDB, `tn_` The Numbers, `wd_` Wikidata, `bom_` Box Office Mojo, `sl_` RT stefanoleone992, `rt_` RT andrezaza, `fin_` combined.
--- 3
## 2. TMDB

All released, non-adult films (one row per id). Matching uses a wider year window (1998–2025) so films near the edges can still match; the contract window is applied after.
--- 4
t = pd.read_csv(RAW / "TMDB_movie_dataset_v11.csv", low_memory=False)
t["release_dt"] = pd.to_datetime(t["release_date"], errors="coerce")
t["year"] = t["release_dt"].dt.year
tmdb = t[t["status"].eq("Released") & ~t["adult"] & t["year"].between(1998, 2025)].drop_duplicates("id").copy()

# Sanity check: Matt's contract population is reproduced exactly
pop = tmdb[tmdb["year"].between(*YEARS) & tmdb["budget"].ge(BUDGET_FLOOR) & tmdb["revenue"].gt(0)]
assert len(pop) == 5766, len(pop)
print(f"TMDB candidates for matching: {len(tmdb):,}; contract population: {len(pop):,}")
--- 28
## 9. One row per film

The sources are joined one-to-one, but TMDB itself sometimes lists the same film twice (and junk entries repeat). Rows are merged when they are the same film by either rule:

1. **Same IMDb id** (`imdb_id`), or
2. **Same normalized title, release year within ±1, runtime within 5 minutes (or unknown on either side: TMDB uses 0 for unknown), and combined budget within 15%.** Title alone isn't enough: remakes and shorts share titles (*Trolls* 2016 at $125M vs a $30K short).

Within a group, the row with the most filled-in values is kept (TMDB rows and usable rows first), and its blanks are filled from the others. `merged_ids` lists the absorbed ids. `usable` is recomputed after merging.

Then each film gets **`film_uid`**: `tmdb-<id>`, or `tn-<The Numbers URL slug>` (e.g. `tn-Marvels-The-(2023)`).
--- 29
unified = films[films["year"].between(*YEARS) & (films["fin_budget"].notna() | films["fin_revenue"].notna())].copy()
unified = unified.reset_index(drop=True)

# Candidate pairs (row positions)
pairs = []
imdb = unified["imdb_id"].where(unified["imdb_id"].astype(str).str.startswith("tt"))
g = unified.assign(imdb=imdb).dropna(subset=["imdb"]).groupby("imdb").groups
pairs += [(ix[0], j) for ix in g.values() if len(ix) > 1 for j in ix[1:]]

k = pd.DataFrame({"pos": unified.index, "key": norm_title(unified["title"]), "year": unified["year"],
                  "rt": unified["runtime"].replace(0, np.nan), "b": unified["fin_budget"]})
k = k[k["key"].ne("")]
pp = k.merge(k, on="key", suffixes=("", "_2"))
runtime_ok = (pp["rt"] - pp["rt_2"]).abs().le(5) | pp["rt"].isna() | pp["rt_2"].isna()   # 0/missing = unknown
pp = pp[(pp["pos"] < pp["pos_2"]) & (pp["year"] - pp["year_2"]).abs().le(1) & runtime_ok
        & ((pp["b"] / pp["b_2"] - 1).abs() < 0.15)]
pairs += list(zip(pp["pos"], pp["pos_2"]))

# Group pairs (union-find)
parent = {}
def find(x):
    while parent.get(x, x) != x:
        x = parent[x]

--- 0
# 01 · Clean the unified dataset

**Shared pipeline notebook (team-owned).** Run it after `00_build_dataset.ipynb`. Changes go through a PR.

**Input:** `data/clean/films_unified.csv` (one row per film, every source's columns side by side).
**Outputs** (gitignored; rebuilt on every run):
- `data/clean/films_clean.csv`: same films and rows, plus one **combined column per fact** (runtime, US release date, rating, genre…), with a `_src` column showing which source supplied the value and a `_missing` flag for inputs that aren't always filled.
- `data/clean/films_clean_columns.csv`: a dictionary giving every column's group and role.

**Why:** each fact (runtime, genre, rating…) comes from several sources, each in its own column. The rules, agreed in `Edwards-A10.ipynb` §4b (Tanner, 2026-11-24), are:

2. Only real values count. TMDB's `0` for budget, revenue or runtime means unknown, and so does Box Office Mojo's `-` distributor.

    if has("based on comic", "superhero", "based on graphic novel", "based on manga", "comic book", "based on webcomic", "based on cartoon"):

| `budget_error` | Over $3M per minute, or under 70 min with a $20M+ budget (except *Winnie the Pooh* and *Pooh's Heffalump Movie*); 4 foreign budgets checked by hand (§8h) |
| `revenue_equals_budget` | Revenue exactly equals the budget: a copied value |
| `tiny_revenue_unrated` | Revenue under $10K and no MPAA rating (NR or blank) |

w = wd.reindex(films["id"].where(films["in_tmdb"]).astype("Int64")).set_index(films.index)


def names(s):
    return [t.strip() for t in str(s).replace("|", ",").split(",") if t.strip()] if pd.notna(s) else []


def norm(n):
    n = unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", n).encode("ascii", "ignore").decode()
    return "".join(ch for ch in n.lower() if ch.isalpha() or ch == " ").split()


def same_person(a, b):
    """Same name ignoring punctuation, accents and order; one name inside the other; same last name; or near-identical."""
    A, B = norm(a), norm(b)
    if not A or not B:
        return False
    if "".join(A) == "".join(B) or set(A) <= set(B) or set(B) <= set(A) or A[-1] == B[-1]:

    return difflib.SequenceMatcher(None, " ".join(sorted(A)), " ".join(sorted(B))).ratio() >= 0.8

    return np.nan

films.loc[gap, "source_material"] = w.loc[gap, "wd_based_on_type"].map(source_from_type)
films.loc[gap, "source_material_src"] = "wikidata"

    if has("remake", "reboot", "based on movie", "based on short film"):
        return "Remake"
    if has("based on true story", "biography", "biographical", "based on memoir", "autobiograph"):

    if has("based on novel", "based on young adult novel", "based on children's book", "based on short story", "based on magazine", "literary adaptation"):

    if has("based on video game", "based on tv series", "based on play", "based on toy", "based on fairy tale", "based on myths",

Why: Matt agreed to all amendments (A5: keep the COVID stress test). The

notebook, and others need to pull and run it easily, so the cleaning
belongs in the pipeline and the master reads its output.

- Contract: A1-A7 copied into the Amendments section (dated, with
  reasons); proposals file marked agreed. Timing rule "controlled before
  release" (A6) updated in CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, FEATURE_IDEAS.md.
- 00_build: include late-2023 films TMDB still listed as in production;
  Wonka, Wish and Five Nights at Freddy's now match their real entries.
- 01_clean (never deletes films): §10b budget repair (TMDB vs The Numbers
  > 2x), §10c Wikidata fills + director same-title fix, §10d source_group,
  §11b rule fills (MPAA -> NR, country from language, franchise none),
  §12 exclude_reason rules, in_population, label loser = US box office
  < 1.25x budget (A7), us_multiple. Budget-per-minute limit raised from
  $3M to $5M so The Force Awakens isn't excluded after its budget repair.
  Result: 6,839 usable -> 5,854 after rules -> 4,933 in population,
  66.9% losers (train 3,708 / test 855 / stress 370).
- A10-master.ipynb: CRISP-DM sections 1 Business Understanding,
  2 Data Understanding (sources, missing values, input EDA, label,
  data-quality problems), 3 Data Preparation (combine, budget repair,
  fills, exclusions, final dataset); 4-6 placeholders. Reads
  films_clean.csv only.
- README: run order and model rows / label.

Next: modeling (baseline genre x budget-tier rule vs model, track-record
features from earlier films only). Open: matcher misses a few big films
(F9, The Butler); company/distributor name grouping.

EOF

+## A8. Change the decision to the studio's pre-release review
+**Proposed by Matt, 2026-11-24. DRAFT, not in effect until Matt and Tanner both approve this wording.** Matt reports that Tanner agrees to the change of question.
+**Question the model answers:** Will this movie be successful, meaning worldwide revenue of at least 2.5× its budget?
+**Decision it supports:** Before release, which upcoming films are most likely to lose money, so the studio can review their release and marketing plans first?

+**Reason:** The team chose to predict a film's success before release instead of whether a financier should agree to make it. The problem scan for candidate #1 already described a decision made "before a film is released"; the frozen contract had narrowed it to financing. At release, more of the film's plan is known and the studio can still change its release and marketing.

+| **Decision** | At financing, flag / proceed / pass | Before release, the studio decides which films get a deeper review of the release plan and marketing plan, and which proceed on standard review |

+| **Action** | 20% highest-risk projects per year go to deep review | Each year, the 20% of films with the highest predicted risk of losing money get the deeper review. The rest proceed as planned. A person makes every final decision. |

+| **Owner** | Head of Acquisitions at a film co-financier | The studio executive responsible for release and marketing. Still a stand-in role with no real stakeholder interviews; the report says so. |
+| **Decision time** | Before production | When the release and marketing plans can still be changed: the film is finished or nearly so, and no public release results exist |
+| **Unit** | One feature film at its financing decision | One feature film at its pre-release review |

+| **Outcome** | Money-loser: worldwide revenue < 2.5× budget | **Same cutoff.** Successful = worldwide revenue ≥ 2.5× budget; money-loser = everything below. The model still ranks by money-loser risk. 2.5× is labeled an industry convention; 1×, 2× and 3× sensitivity checks stay. |

+| **Allowed inputs** | 8 inputs known at financing | The same 8, using values known before release, plus MPAA rating, distributor, writer, source material, creative type, production method and franchise (conditions below) |

+| **Value** | Loss avoided on flagged deals | (extra money-losers caught × loss avoided per film by a changed plan × share of flagged plans changed) − (successful films flagged × cost of an unneeded review). Every term stays a blank for the owner; the report shows break-even values. |
+| **Rival framing** | Director premium | The original financing screen, limited to inputs known before production |
+- **Franchise:** count a film as franchise only if an earlier film in that franchise had been released. Source data tags first films in hindsight (*Iron Man*, 2008).
+- **Track records:** use only films released before this one.
+- **Coverage:** MPAA rating, source material and creative type are often blank for small films, so each carries a missing flag. No rows are dropped for blanks.

+- **Still prohibited:** box office, opening results, scores, votes, popularity, all reviews (including pre-release reviews), festival buzz and TMDB keywords. Keywords can't be used to fill another input either.
+2. **Automatic reject** becomes: never an automatic cancellation, shelving or marketing cut.
+3. **Causal claim** also covers release and marketing: the model shows which films are risky, not that changing the plan would fix them. The data has no marketing spend.
+- The production budget is already spent by this point. The screen can only improve what is still undecided.
+- The data records what finally happened (date, distributor, rating), which may differ from the plan at review time. Weakest link 4 is reduced, not removed.

+Population years and the $1M floor, the training / test / stress periods, baselines (a) and (b), the ≥ 5-point evidence bar, 20% capacity, and stop conditions S1–S4. Cleaning rules can't drop films because of their outcome (for example, only those with low revenue).
+| Proposal | Effect if A8 is approved |
+| A3 | Accepted in substance (keep 2.5×, labeled a convention) |
+| A4 | Resolved by the input list above |
+| A6 | Replaced by A8's decision time |
+| A7 (US box office < 1.25×) | Not adopted as the main outcome or population. Can run as a sensitivity check. **Tanner to confirm.** |
+| A1, A2, A5 | Not affected; still need a decision |
+| Budgets and revenue from The Numbers / Wikidata | Not covered here; needs its own amendment |
+### What had been seen before this amendment

+No model had been fitted. The following had been looked at: loser rates overall and by period (**including the 2016–2019 test films**), by financial source, by Rotten Tomatoes match status, and for US and non-US films; returns for budgets below and above $1M; and a budget vs revenue chart. The success cutoff and evidence bar did not change.

| **Decision** | At financing, flag / proceed / pass | Before release, the studio decides which films get a deeper review of the release plan and marketing plan, and which proceed on standard review |
| **Action** | 20% highest-risk projects per year go to deep review | Each year, the 20% of films with the highest predicted risk of losing money get the deeper review. The rest proceed as planned. A person makes every final decision. |
| **Owner** | Head of Acquisitions at a film co-financier | The studio executive responsible for release and marketing. Still a stand-in role with no real stakeholder interviews; the report says so. |
| **Decision time** | Before production | When the release and marketing plans can still be changed: the film is finished or nearly so, and no public release results exist |
| **Unit** | One feature film at its financing decision | One feature film at its pre-release review |
| **Outcome** | Money-loser: worldwide revenue < 2.5× budget | **Same cutoff.** Successful = worldwide revenue ≥ 2.5× budget; money-loser = everything below. The model still ranks by money-loser risk. 2.5× is labeled an industry convention; 1×, 2× and 3× sensitivity checks stay. |
| **Allowed inputs** | 8 inputs known at financing | The same 8, using values known before release, plus MPAA rating, distributor, writer, source material, creative type, production method and franchise (conditions below) |
| **Value** | Loss avoided on flagged deals | (extra money-losers caught × loss avoided per film by a changed plan × share of flagged plans changed) − (successful films flagged × cost of an unneeded review). Every term stays a blank for the owner; the report shows break-even values. |
| **Rival framing** | Director premium | The original financing screen, limited to inputs known before production |

### Input conditions
- **Franchise:** count a film as franchise only if an earlier film in that franchise had been released. Source data tags first films in hindsight (*Iron Man*, 2008).
- **Track records:** use only films released before this one.
- **Coverage:** MPAA rating, source material and creative type are often blank for small films, so each carries a missing flag. No rows are dropped for blanks.
- **Still prohibited:** box office, opening results, scores, votes, popularity, all reviews (including pre-release reviews), festival buzz and TMDB keywords. Keywords can't be used to fill another input either.

### Prohibited uses
1. **Hiring or blacklisting people:** unchanged.
2. **Automatic reject** becomes: never an automatic cancellation, shelving or marketing cut.
3. **Causal claim** also covers release and marketing: the model shows which films are risky, not that changing the plan would fix them. The data has no marketing spend.
4. **Outside its population:** unchanged.

### Limitations to report
- The production budget is already spent by this point. The screen can only improve what is still undecided.
- The data records what finally happened (date, distributor, rating), which may differ from the plan at review time. Weakest link 4 is reduced, not removed.

### What stays the same
Population years and the $1M floor, the training / test / stress periods, baselines (a) and (b), the ≥ 5-point evidence bar, 20% capacity, and stop conditions S1–S4. Cleaning rules can't drop films because of their outcome (for example, only those with low revenue).

### Effect on the other proposals
| Proposal | Effect if A8 is approved |
|---|---|
| A3 | Accepted in substance (keep 2.5×, labeled a convention) |
| A4 | Resolved by the input list above |
| A6 | Replaced by A8's decision time |
| A7 (US box office < 1.25×) | Not adopted as the main outcome or population. Can run as a sensitivity check. **Tanner to confirm.** |
| A1, A2, A5 | Not affected; still need a decision |
| Budgets and revenue from The Numbers / Wikidata | Not covered here; needs its own amendment |

### What had been seen before this amendment
No model had been fitted. The following had been looked at: loser rates overall and by period (**including the 2016–2019 test films**), by financial source, by Rotten Tomatoes match status, and for US and non-US films; returns for budgets below and above $1M; and a budget vs revenue chart. The success cutoff and evidence bar did not change.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /private/tmp/claude-503/bundled-skills/2.1.325/11c07dee2358ae613450374ce5a258b5/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
   One exception to direct name labels: the tall segmented bar (*Figures* in `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`).
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
  One exception, legend kept: the tall segmented bar (*Figures* in `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`).
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical, except that dark-mode good is the series green |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |
I'll create the branch, then load the charting guidance before writing any charts.

People and companies can't be compared by name (most appear once), so §10d uses **experience**: how many earlier films the person or company had, counted from release dates (earlier films only, so no peeking ahead).'''),
C('''from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint

clean_now = pd.read_csv("../data/clean/films_clean.csv", low_memory=False)
clean_now["release_date"] = pd.to_datetime(clean_now["release_date"], format="mixed", errors="coerce")
tr = clean_now[clean_now["in_population"] & clean_now["year"].le(2015)].copy()
tr["loser"] = tr["loser"].astype(bool)
BASE = tr["loser"].mean()
print(f"Training films: {len(tr):,}; loser rate {BASE:.1%}")

SIGNAL = []   # (input, spread in percentage points between the highest and lowest group with 30+ films)


def rate_table(groups, min_n=30, order=None):
    g = pd.DataFrame({"g": groups, "y": tr.loc[groups.index, "loser"] if isinstance(groups, pd.Series) else tr["loser"]})
    t = g.groupby("g", observed=True)["y"].agg(films="size", losers="sum")
    t = t[t["films"] >= min_n]
    if order is not None:
        t = t.reindex([o for o in order if o in t.index])
    lo, hi = proportion_confint(t["losers"], t["films"], method="wilson")
    t["rate"], t["lo"], t["hi"] = t["losers"] / t["films"], lo, hi
    return t


def rate_plot(ax, groups, title, min_n=30, order=None, sort=False, horizontal=False, record=None):
    t = rate_table(groups, min_n, order)
    if sort:
        t = t.sort_values("rate")
    x = np.arange(len(t))
    err = [100 * (t["rate"] - t["lo"]), 100 * (t["hi"] - t["rate"])]
    if horizontal:
        ax.barh(x, 100 * t["rate"], color=BLUE, height=0.7, xerr=err, error_kw={"ecolor": INK2, "lw": 0.8})
        ax.axvline(100 * BASE, color="#9a9890", lw=1, ls="--")
        ax.set_yticks(x, [f"{i}  (n={n:,})" for i, n in zip(t.index, t["films"])])
        ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_xlabel("loser rate (%)")
    else:
        ax.bar(x, 100 * t["rate"], color=BLUE, width=0.7, yerr=err, error_kw={"ecolor": INK2, "lw": 0.8})
        ax.axhline(100 * BASE, color="#9a9890", lw=1, ls="--")
        ax.set_xticks(x, [f"{i}\\nn={n:,}" for i, n in zip(t.index, t["films"])])
        ax.set_ylim(0, 100); ax.set_ylabel("loser rate (%)")
    ax.set_title(title)
    if record:
        SIGNAL.append({"input": record, "groups": len(t), "lowest group": f"{t['rate'].idxmin()} ({t['rate'].min():.0%})",
                       "highest group": f"{t['rate'].idxmax()} ({t['rate'].max():.0%})",
                       "spread (pts)": round(100 * (t["rate"].max() - t["rate"].min()), 1)})
    return t'''),
M('### 10a. Money and timing: budget, runtime, release month, quarter, year'),
C('''fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(15, 8))
btier = pd.cut(tr["fin_budget"], [0, 5e6, 10e6, 20e6, 40e6, 80e6, np.inf], labels=["$1-5M", "$5-10M", "$10-20M", "$20-40M", "$40-80M", "$80M+"])
rate_plot(ax[0, 0], btier, "Budget tier", record="budget")
rbin = pd.cut(tr["runtime_min"], [0, 85, 95, 105, 115, 130, np.inf], labels=["<85", "85-94", "95-104", "105-114", "115-129", "130+"], right=False)
rate_plot(ax[0, 1], rbin, "Runtime (minutes)", record="runtime_min")
rate_plot(ax[0, 2], tr["release_month"].astype(int), "Release month", record="release_month")
rate_plot(ax[1, 0], tr["release_quarter"].astype(int).map(lambda q: f"Q{q}"), "Release quarter", record="release_quarter")
dow = tr["release_date"].dt.day_name().where(lambda s: s.isin(["Wednesday", "Friday"]), "Other day")
rate_plot(ax[1, 1], dow, "Release day of week", order=["Wednesday", "Friday", "Other day"], record="release day of week")
rate_plot(ax[1, 2], tr["year"].astype(int), "Release year (training years)", min_n=30)
ax[1, 2].tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()'''),
M('### 10b. Content: MPAA rating, genre, source, creative type, franchise'),
C('''fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(15, 10))
rate_plot(ax[0, 0], tr["mpaa_rating"].where(~tr["mpaa_rating_missing"], "blank (filled NR)"), "MPAA rating",
          order=["G", "PG", "PG-13", "R", "NC-17", "NR", "blank (filled NR)"], record="mpaa_rating")
gen = tr["genres_all"].str.split(",").explode().str.strip().dropna()
rate_plot(ax[0, 1], gen, "Genre (a film counts in each of its genres)", sort=True, horizontal=True, record="genres_all")
rate_plot(ax[1, 0], tr["source_group"].fillna("(blank)"), "Source material group (Tanner's hypothesis)", sort=True, horizontal=True, record="source_group")
rate_plot(ax[1, 1], tr["creative_type"].fillna("(blank)"), "Creative type", sort=True, horizontal=True, record="creative_type")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()'''),

rate_plot(ax[1], np.select([prior, fr], ["sequel / later film", "first film of a franchise"], "no franchise").astype(object).__array__() and

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()'''),

cgroup = np.select([us.eq("United States of America"), us.str.contains("United States")], ["US only", "US co-production"], "non-US")

import pandas as pd, numpy as np
d=pd.read_csv('data/clean/films_clean.csv',low_memory=False); d['release_date']=pd.to_datetime(d.release_date,format='mixed',errors='coerce')
tr=d[d.in_population & d.year.le(2015)].copy(); tr['loser']=tr.loser.astype(bool)
allf=d[d.usable & d.exclude_reason.isna() & d.franchise.ne('(none)')][['franchise','release_date']]
first=allf.assign(f=allf.franchise.str.split('|')).explode('f').groupby('f').release_date.min()

fr=tr.franchise.ne('(none)')
g=np.select([prior,fr],['sequel','first','none'])
print(tr.groupby(g).loser.agg(['size','mean']))
us=tr.countries.fillna('')
cg=np.select([us.eq('United States of America'),us.str.contains('United States')],['US only','US co'],'non-US')
print(tr.groupby(cg).loser.agg(['size','mean']))
print(tr.groupby(tr.mpaa_rating).loser.agg(['size','mean']))
print("NR/blank share of nonUS:", tr[cg=='non-US'].mpaa_rating.eq('NR').mean())
EOF

import nbformat
p='notebooks/Edwards-A10.ipynb'
nb=nbformat.read(p,4)
md='''### 10g. What the label comparisons show (run 2026-11-24, training years only)

Overall: 3,708 training films, 66.9% losers.

**Strong signals**
1. **MPAA rating:** G 48% → PG 56% → PG-13 60% → R 70% → **NR 98%**. 80% of NR films are non-US; NR mostly means a foreign or limited release.
2. **Origin:** US-only films 58%, US co-productions 70%, **non-US 90%**. Language says the same (English 63%, not English 90%). Under a US box-office label, foreign films rarely earn back their budget in the US.
3. **Sequels:** films with an earlier film in the same franchise already released lose **42%** of the time, vs 74% for non-franchise films.
4. **Genre:** Western 89%, War 86%, History 82% at the top; Family 53%, Documentary 51%, Animation 59%, Horror 59% at the bottom.
5. **Distributor:** Warner Bros. 51% at the low end, IFC Films 92% at the high end (names not yet standardized).
6. **Creative type:** Kids Fiction 52%, Super Hero 55%, Factual 52%; Historical Fiction 76%.

**Weak signals:** budget tier (61–74%, no straight line), runtime (59–71%), release month (61–73%; Sep and May worst, Jun and Aug best), quarter (65–68%). Wednesday releases lose less (57%) than Friday (69%), likely because big films open midweek on holidays.

**Tanner's source hypothesis:** only partly supported. Comic 65%, Remake 63%, Original 67%, Book 70%: the groups sit within a few points of each other and their intervals overlap. Other adaptation (TV, games, toys) is lowest at 58%. Creative type's Super Hero (55%) and Kids Fiction (52%) separate better than source group does.

**Experience:** directors and writers with earlier films lose a little less (62–64% vs 70% for a first film). Production companies with 10+ earlier films: 61% vs 72–81% for less experienced ones.

**⚠️ Two warnings before these become model inputs**
- **Blanks predict losers too well (84–100%).** A blank usually means the databases never documented the film, and they document successful films better. So a blank partly records the outcome. The `_missing` flags (and "blank" groups) may leak the label; test the model with and without them.
- **"First film of a franchise" is hindsight.** Those films lose only 33%, because a film only becomes the first of a franchise *after* it succeeds and gets sequels. Only "an earlier film was already released" (sequel) is known before release (matches Matt's A8 condition).
'''
nb.cells.append(nbformat.v4.new_markdown_cell(md))
nbformat.write(nb,p)
EOF
echo ok

content.text:
Because the contract's decision is about catching risky films, and the two labels are just flip sides of each other.

- **It's the same split.** Every film is either a loser or a winner, so the winner rate is 100% minus the loser rate. A genre with 70% losers has 30% winners, so every chart would look the same, just flipped.
- **The decision is about catching risk.** The screen flags the 20% riskiest films for a deeper review, and success is measured by how many losers land in that flagged 20%. So "loser" is what the model has to find.

One reason to reconsider: losers are the majority, at 67% of films. Finding the 33% of winners is the rarer, arguably more valuable target, and it's how Matt's A8 phrases the question: "will this movie be successful?" If you'd rather present it as "what makes a winner," I can flip the charts to winner rates. The data and the model stay the same; only the wording changes.

    s=s.replace('"loser rate (%)"','"winner rate (%)"')

    s=s.replace('sort_values("difference (pts)", ascending=False)','sort_values("difference (pts)")')

for c in sec:

I changed §10 to compare each input with the return: **US box office ÷ budget**. Release year is out of the charts and marked "not a model input."

**How to read the charts:** each row is a group. The dot is the median return, and the bar covers the middle half of its films. The dashed line at 1.25× is the winner line. Across all training films, the median return is 0.72×.

**What changed versus the winner rate**
- **Your source-material hypothesis holds up.** Comic (0.96×), Remake (0.95×) and Other adaptation (1.06×) return about 40% more than Original screenplays (0.67×). The winner rate hid this: the groups differ in how *much* they make, more than in how *often* they clear 1.25×.
- **Budget now shows a clear pattern.** Films under $10M return a median 0.24–0.27×, against 0.78–0.99× above $10M.

**Strongest signals**

| Input | Best → worst median return |
|---|---|
| MPAA rating | G 1.31× → R 0.56× → NR 0.05× |
| Origin | US-only 1.02× → non-US 0.11× |
| Franchise | sequel 1.45× vs no franchise 0.54× |
| Genre | Family 1.17× → War 0.32× |
| Director experience | first film 0.57× → 10+ earlier films 1.07× |

Both warnings still hold:
- Films with blank fields return almost nothing, a median of 0.03–0.14×. That likely reflects which films got documented, not a real signal.
- "First film of a franchise" is hindsight: a film only becomes a franchise's first after it succeeds.

content.text:
They're there, but easy to miss. Section §10d, "People and companies: experience from earlier films," has three small charts side by side, titled "director: earlier films," "writer: earlier films" and "production_companies: earlier films." They show the director movie count, with one difference: they count only the films a director had made **before** this one, not their total in the dataset.

| Director's earlier films | Median return |
|---|---|
| 0 (first film) | 0.57× |
| 1 | 0.81× |
| 2–4 | 0.89× |
| 5–9 | 1.01× |

More experience means better returns. Directors with 10+ earlier films don't get a bar because fewer than 30 training films have one.

**Why earlier films only:** total film count is time travel, the same problem as release year. Christopher Nolan's 2000 film *Memento* would get credit for the hits he made afterward. At decision time, the studio only knows a director's past.

The problem is presentation: three cramped charts with code-style titles, and no director/writer/company headings in the outline. Do you want me to split them into their own clearly titled sections with bigger charts? I can also add a "total films in the dataset" view next to each, labeled as hindsight, so you can see how much the time travel would inflate the signal.

message.content: help me understand 10e

content.text:
§10e asks one question: **do films with a blank field do worse than films where that field is filled?**

For each input, the table splits the training films into two groups, blank and filled, and compares their median return (US box office ÷ budget):

| Input | Films blank | Median if blank | Median if filled | Filled ÷ blank |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| source_group | 65 | 0.03× | 0.74× | 26× |
| mpaa_rating | 100 | 0.06× | 0.75× | 13× |
| creative_type | 606 | 0.07× | 0.90× | 12× |
| distributor | 334 | 0.07× | 0.80× | 11× |
| director | 67 | 0.11× | 0.73× | 7× |
| franchise | 3,025 | 0.54× | 1.60× | 3× |

**How to read a row:** the 65 films with no source material on record earned a median 3 cents per budget dollar in the US. Films with it on record earned 74 cents. So the filled films did 26 times better.

**What it means:** across every input, a blank marks a flop. That's not because missing data causes failure. It's because of who documents films. The Numbers, Rotten Tomatoes and Wikidata fill in details for films people paid attention to, and a film that bombed or barely opened in the US often never gets its rating, distributor or source written down. So the blank is partly a **result** of the outcome.

**Why it matters:** if the model uses "was blank" as an input, it will look very accurate, but partly because it's reading the answer. A brand-new film being reviewed before release won't have that clue yet.

**Franchise is the exception.** A blank there means "not in a franchise," a real fact rather than missing data. Its gap (0.54× vs 1.60×) is a genuine signal.

**Takeaway:** don't trust the "was blank" flags as inputs. Build the model with them and without them. If accuracy drops a lot without them, the flags were leaking the outcome.

content.text:
I added §11 to your notebook with all six deep dives, using training years only, and ran it.

**Top three distributors** (Warner Bros., 20th Century Fox, Sony, with name variants merged):
- Median return 0.99–1.17×, against 0.72× overall.
- Bigger budgets: median $32–42M vs $20M.
- Mostly PG-13 (43–55%), almost never NR, more action and adventure, less drama.
- Fox runs shorter and more family; Warner runs longer and more R and crime.

**G-rated films:** as you guessed, 82% are family and 57% animated, and half come from Disney. They're the shortest films (median 88 minutes), with a median return of 1.31×.

**Budget vs return:** more money does **not** guarantee a bigger multiple.
- Above about $10M, the median return flattens near 0.8–1.0×. What the extra budget buys is a narrower spread, meaning less risk.
- Under $10M, most films earn back little in US theaters, but a few return 10× or more.
- **In dollars:** the median film loses money in the US in every budget tier. The 1.25× line means a $3M film needs $3.8M in US box office; a $125M film needs $156M.
- The upside grows with budget: the top-quarter profit is $1M for small films vs $62M for $80M+ films.

**Documentaries:** the high median comes from cheap budgets (median $2.5M), so a modest gross is a big multiple. The wide spread comes from two kinds of film sharing the label:
- wide-release crowd-pleasers: *Jackass*, stand-up comedy films, *March of the Penguins*, and concert films, which have a median of 2.89×
- limited-release issue documentaries that earn almost nothing

**Release month, sorted best to worst:** June, December and July are best; September, October and May are worst.

**First films of franchises** (known only in hindsight): they look like sequels, not like typical films. Compared with non-franchise films they are:
- more family, action and adventure
- more PG
- more often based on games, TV, toys or comics
- bigger-budget, from the majors, released in summer

We already have all of those as inputs, so the model can learn "looks like a franchise starter" without the hindsight tag.

**One data problem:** our data starts in 2000, so some "first films" are really sequels to older films, like *Toy Story 3* and *Mission: Impossible II*. I noted the fix (installment numbers from the title or Wikidata) under the sequel idea in `FEATURE_IDEAS.md`.

content.text:
It's true for a handful of huge franchises, but not for animated G films in general. And no, there isn't much we can use directly.

**What's true:** for a few franchises, toy and merchandise sales dwarf the box office. *Cars* is the classic case. Disney reported about $10B in global retail sales over five years, while all three *Cars* films together made about $1.4B worldwide at the box office. The first film was a relatively weak performer at the box office; the merchandise drove the sequels. *Frozen* is similar.

**The catch:**
- **Retail sales aren't studio revenue.** The studio only gets a licensing royalty, around 9% of sales on average and sometimes 20%+ for character brands. So $10B in toy sales is closer to $1B for Disney: comparable to the box office, not several times it.
- **It's a few mega-hits, not the typical animated film.** Most never sell much merchandise.

**Can we use it?** Not as data: none of our sources has merchandise numbers. It matters for the report in two ways:
- **It's a limitation of our label.** We count US box office only, so a family film we call a "loser" might still make the studio money through toys, home video or streaming. The report should say so.
- **We already capture the "toy-friendly" signal with existing inputs:** Kids Fiction, Animation, G/PG, "based on a toy," and a major studio. A separate feature would add little.

I logged it in `FEATURE_IDEAS.md` as low priority, mainly as a limitation to state in the report.

**Has return gone down?** Yes, then partly back. Median return: 0.84× in 2000–05 → 0.64–0.67× in 2006–15 → 0.76× in 2016–19 (test) → 0.59× in 2020–23 (COVID; 2020 alone 0.35×). Winners: 37% → 31–32% → 36% → 26%. In 2023 dollars, the typical film's budget and US box office both fell by about half from 2000 to 2015. Caution: part of this is **which films are in the data** (more small and foreign films get recorded in later years), not only the market. A model trained on 2000–15 will meet a somewhat different mix in 2016–19, and a very different one in 2020–23 (A5 stress test).

**Distributors by median return:** Disney is first (1.28×, 53% winners), then Paramount, Sony, Fox and Universal (1.16–1.19×). **Warner Bros. distributes the most films but ranks 11th (0.99×).** The specialty and indie labels sit at the bottom: Sony Pictures Classics 0.29×, Roadside 0.15×, IFC and Magnolia 0.02× (they release small films in few US theaters, often after a festival or alongside video on demand).

**Big budget at a lower return vs small budget at a higher return** (2023 dollars; profit = US box office − budget):
- **Per film, bigger makes more money.** Average profit per film rises from $3M ($1–5M films) to $21M ($80M+ films). Tanner's example holds: *Ocean's Twelve* at 1.1× made $25M; *The Squid and the Whale* at 4.9× made $9M.
- **Per dollar invested, small films return more on average.** $100 spread across $1–5M films brings back $212 in US box office, vs $114 across $80M+ films.
- **But small films are a lottery.** That average comes from rare breakouts: 69–74% of films under $10M don't earn back their budget, vs 52–55% above $40M. The *typical* film loses money in every tier.
- **Answer:** if the studio can make many small films, the portfolio returns more per dollar (a few hits pay for many flops). For any **single** film, the bigger budget makes more dollars and is slightly less likely to lose money. Big films also carry the biggest absolute losses, and marketing (not in our data) scales with budget.

**R-rated comedies in franchises:** Tanner's read is **partly right**.
- Among **sequels**, R comedy is 5th (1.85×, 70% winners). Ahead of it: PG-13 romance (2.52×, the *Twilight* films), PG-13 drama and comedy, and R horror (2.00×). PG-13 action isn't near the top; PG-13 sci-fi and thriller sit around 1.3×.
- Among **all franchise films** (with first films, hindsight), R comedy is 4th (2.49×, 77% winners).
- **Share of the group:** R comedies are only **8% of sequels (23 films)** and 9% of all franchise films (64).
- **Always a solid investment? No.** The safety comes from being a sequel, not from R comedy. R comedies **outside a franchise** (443 films) have a median of 0.57× and only 30% winners. content.text:
I added §12 to your notebook with the four analyses, and dollar amounts in 2023 dollars.

**1. Has return gone down? Yes, then partly back.** These are medians across all 2000–2023 films:

| Period | Median return | Winners |
|---|---|---|
| 2000–05 | 0.84× | 37% |
| 2006–15 | 0.64–0.67× | 31–32% |
| 2016–19 | 0.76× | 36% |
| 2020–23 (COVID) | 0.59× | 26% |

In 2023 dollars, the typical budget and US box office both roughly halved from 2000 to 2015. Part of that is a change in which films are in the data: more small and foreign films were recorded in later years.

**2. Distributors ranked by median return:** Disney is first (1.28×), then Paramount, Sony, Fox and Universal (about 1.16–1.19×). **Warner Bros. releases the most films but ranks only 11th (0.99×).** The indie labels sit at the bottom: IFC and Magnolia at 0.02×.

**3. Big budget at a lower return vs small budget at a higher return:**
- **Per film, bigger makes more money.** Average US profit rises from $3M for $1–5M films to $21M for $80M+ films. Your example holds: *Ocean's Twelve* returned 1.1× and made $25M; *The Squid and the Whale* returned 4.9× and made $9M.
- **Per dollar invested, small films return more on average:** $100 spread across $1–5M films brings back $212, against $114 for $80M+ films.
- **But small films are a lottery.** About 70% of films under $10M don't earn back their budget, against about 53% above $40M. A few breakouts carry the average.
- **The answer:** a studio making many small films gets more per dollar. For a single film, the big budget makes more dollars and is a little less likely to lose money.

**4. R-rated comedies in franchises: partly right.**
- They rank 5th among sequels (1.85×, 70% winners). Ahead of them are PG-13 romance (*Madea*, *Twilight*), PG-13 drama and comedy, and R horror. PG-13 action isn't near the top; PG-13 sci-fi and thriller sit around 1.3×.
- They're only **8% of sequels** (23 films).
- **Not always a solid investment.** The safety comes from being a sequel. R comedies outside a franchise (443 films) have a median return of 0.57× and only 30% winners. Even sequels flop sometimes: *Sex and the City 2*, *Hot Tub Time Machine 2*.

Nothing is committed yet.

- **Remakes** were strong early (1.24×) but swing a lot (0.46× in 2012–15).

- **Comedy** sits above the market in every period (0.79–1.12×). **Drama** sits below it in every period (0.32–0.67×).

I added §12f with trend charts and §12g with the findings. They cover 2000–2023 in 4-year periods. Each group is its own small chart, compared with the overall market line, with a table of the numbers underneath.

**Rising**
- **Horror** is the clearest trend: about 1× until 2015, then **2.03× in 2016–19** and 1.55× during COVID. It held up best of any genre. Mystery rose with it.
- **G-rated** films are the best rating in every period.
- **Comic** adaptations dipped in 2008–11, then rebounded to 1.32× in 2016–19.

**Falling**
- **Family** films lost their edge: 1.61× in 2000–03, then 0.98×, then 0.73× in 2020–23.
- **Adventure** and **Action** slid steadily.

**Steady**
- **Comedy** sits above the market in every period, and **Drama** below it in every period.
- **Sequels** keep a big premium in every period (1.2–1.8× vs about 0.5× for non-franchise films). Their share of releases grew from 3% to 21%, partly because our data can't recognize sequels to pre-2000 films.
- **Big budgets** ($40M+) held steady until COVID, then fell hardest.

**What it means for the model:** 2016–19, the test period, mostly looks like 2012–15 except for the horror jump. So a model trained on 2000–15 may underrate horror. 2020–23 differs on almost everything, which supports keeping it as a separate stress test.

- the film has a franchise tag (*Toy Story 3*), or
- an **earlier** film exists under the title with the number removed (*Paddington 2* → *Paddington*), checked against all of TMDB, including pre-2000 films.'''),
C('''tm = pd.read_csv("../data/raw/TMDB_movie_dataset_v11.csv", usecols=["title", "release_date", "vote_count"], low_memory=False)
tm = tm[tm["vote_count"].fillna(0) >= 20]                     # real releases, not stray entries
tm["base"] = tm["title"].str.lower().str.strip()
tm["rd"] = pd.to_datetime(tm["release_date"], errors="coerce")
earliest = tm.groupby("base")["rd"].min()


def base_title(t):

    return t.strip().lower()

base = u["title"].map(base_title)

u["title_sequel_v2"] = u["title_says_sequel"] & (explicit | u["franchise"].ne("(none)") | pd.Series(earlier_base, index=u.index))
u["sequel_any"] = u["prior_in_data"] | u["title_sequel_v2"]

]

- **What:** Track whether a film belongs to a series of installments and which installment it is, plus whether it belongs to a wider franchise. *Spider-Man* (2002): first installment of the Spider-Man series. *Iron Man* (2008): first installment of the Iron Man series and part of the Marvel Cinematic Universe franchise.

- **Pre-2000 predecessors (found 2026-11-26, Edwards §11f):** our data starts in 2000, so a sequel whose earlier films are pre-2000 looks like a first film (*Toy Story 3*, *Mission: Impossible II*). | Year | Under $10M | $10–40M | $40M+ | Total | Median return |

| 2010 | 89 | 94 | 62 | 245 | 0.57× |
| 2011 | 83 | 103 | 63 | 249 | 0.62× |
| 2017 | 78 | 82 | 50 | 210 | 0.81× |
| 2018 | 75 | 77 | 54 | 206 | 0.89× |
| 2019 | 59 | 70 | 54 | 183 | 0.87× |

**The recession:** the total stayed flat, about 250 a year, and 2009–10 had some of the *lowest* returns. There is one lagged effect: mid-budget films ($10–40M) fell from 119 in 2008 to 94 in 2010, but more small films replaced them. So no bigger share per film in 2009–10.

**My correction:** the drop to 183 films by 2019 is almost all **small and mid-budget films**. Big films stayed flat at about 50–55 a year, and films grossing $10M+ in the US barely changed. The small films that dropped out had captured almost none of the $14B anyway, so it isn't really "the same pie split across fewer films." The median rose mostly because **fewer low-return small films are in the mix**, which is a composition effect.

There's a data caveat too. Industry-wide, the number of US releases didn't fall in the late 2010s. So part of the drop may be our sources recording fewer small recent films, not fewer being made.
